title: Protein and Nutrition Basics
subtitle: Choose everyday food with more confidence and less label confusion.

blocks.text: Some food packages give protein such large letters that the peas inside seem to need an agent. The useful details are usually quieter, and learning where to look can make shopping easier.
What you will learn

items.title: Explain where protein fits in a varied eating pattern.
Compare food labels without confusing grams and percentages.
Choose practical protein foods, including plant options.
Write one small food decision you can use in your own routine.

blocks.text: Your body uses protein to build and maintain tissues, including muscles. Protein is a nutrient, which means something in food that your body needs; it is not only a product sold in a tub.
Food choices work together across days and weeks. This regular mix is your eating pattern, and it includes vegetables, fruit, whole grains and protein foods.

Carbohydrates supply energy and are found in foods such as rice, potatoes and fruit. Fibre is a type of carbohydrate in plant foods, including beans and whole grains; it supports bowel health. Fats also supply energy and help you absorb some nutrients, and foods such as nuts and canola oil provide unsaturated fats.
Beans, tofu, eggs and yogurt can all fit into everyday meals. Choose foods you enjoy and can access, and include plant protein foods often; a familiar meal can be a useful starting point.

This course offers general food education, not a personal protein target. If you have a prescribed diet, food allergies or questions about your needs, ask a registered dietitian or your health care provider before changing that plan.
Make everyday choices clearer
blocks.detail: Recognise protein foods within a complete meal. This gives you a useful starting point before a package makes its sales pitch.

blocks.text: Start with a food you actually use, such as a breakfast cereal or canned soup. When comparing similar products, check the amount each label describes before comparing their numbers.
The Nutrition Facts table gives protein in grams for its listed serving size. That serving is a label reference, not an instruction about the portion you must eat.
Use a fair comparison. If two packages describe different amounts of food, compare the same amount before deciding which has more protein.
A small label calculation
Here is an illustrative, made-up label: a bean mixture lists 8 g of protein per 125 mL. If you eat 250 mL of that mixture, the amount is twice the labelled serving, so it provides 16 g of protein.
This calculation tells you what is in that portion, not whether it meets your personal needs. The example is for learning label maths and does not describe a real brand.
Read the right unit. Protein grams describe an amount; a percent daily value shown for another nutrient is not a protein amount or your personal protein target.
Percent daily value, or % DV, helps show whether a labelled serving has a little or a lot of certain nutrients. Health Canada uses 5% DV or less for a little and 15% DV or more for a lot.

Look at the food beyond its protein line, including sodium, fibre and saturated fat. Ingredients appear in order by weight, with the largest amounts first; also check allergy information that matters to you.

items.title: “The package with the biggest protein number is always the best choice.”
items.text: The amount described, the rest of the food and how it fits your meal also matter.

blocks.text: Vitamins and minerals have important jobs too. For example, vitamin D helps your body use calcium, a mineral that supports bones and teeth. One food cannot cover every need, which is why the mix you eat matters.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: The lunch that travelled

blocks.text: The lunch that travelled
paragraphs: Edmonton transit driver Farid wanted a lunch he could enjoy during his split shift without buying another snack at the depot. He joked that the shiny protein display at his grocery store looked ready to run for office.

One evening, a large protein claim on a soup pouch caught his eye. He bought it with bread, expecting the pouch to be his whole lunch, but later noticed the Nutrition Facts table described only part of its contents.

Farid read the actual label again and worked out the numbers for what he ate. He still liked the soup, but realised that a bigger protein total did not tell him whether the lunch would suit his appetite or his break.

At home, he compared another soup using an equal amount and looked at sodium too. He decided to keep the first soup for occasional use and try a chickpea wrap with vegetables and fruit on his next shift.

He packed the wrap the night before and kept the filling chilled until his break. The food worked well, but the container did not: it was too wide for his lunch bag and squeezed the wrap against his water bottle.
Instead of buying a special meal kit, Farid used a narrower container he already owned. Over two more shifts, he adjusted how much he packed and added a snack when he wanted one.

His lunch routine still needed attention when his schedule changed, but he now had a meal he could carry and a way to read a label. At the next grocery visit, the protein display kept its campaign promises to itself while Farid checked the details.

blocks.text: Fit food to your real day
blocks.detail: A clear label check and a practical packing choice can help you build a lunch you will actually use. You can adjust the routine without buying a whole new system.

blocks.text: Solve the actual obstacle. A useful food choice still needs a workable container, a suitable storage plan and time to eat it.
Choose one meal that feels awkward. Name the obstacle first, such as food that is hard to carry or a recipe that takes too long.
Adjustable example: Build a bowl
This bowl is an educational example, not a personal meal prescription. Choose suitable foods from what you have and compare one useful label.

items.title: Start with chickpeas, cooked brown rice and vegetables you enjoy.
Chickpeas contribute protein and fibre; rice supplies carbohydrate, and vegetables add variety.
Add a suitable dressing, such as canola oil with lemon and herbs, for flavour and unsaturated fat.
Compare similar chickpea products in equal amounts, including sodium, and plan where the meal will stay chilled.

blocks.text: Keep an easy plant option nearby. Canned beans can save preparation time; low-sodium versions are an option, and draining and rinsing canned beans can reduce sodium.
Swap chickpeas for another suitable protein food if needed. Adjust the amount to your circumstances, and simplify the meal if equipment is limited.
Frozen vegetables can help when winter shopping is difficult. Change one part of your routine at a time to see what helps.
Plan food safety too. Refrigerate leftovers promptly, use them within 2 to 3 days or freeze them, and reheat to 74°C, checked with a digital food thermometer.

Throw away cooked food left at room temperature for more than two hours. Its smell cannot confirm safety, and a cold Canadian day does not make an uncontrolled car or outdoor space a reliable refrigerator.

items.title: “Learning about protein means everyone needs a protein supplement.”
items.text: Supplements are not an automatic requirement; first consider your eating pattern and seek individual advice if you are unsure about your needs.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Write a replacement next to one shopping item, such as chickpeas or lentils. It gives you a practical choice when the shelf is empty, without changing the whole meal.
Quick Check

items.title: Does a labelled serving size tell you how much you must eat?
items.text: It tells you the food amount described by the table.

items.title: An illustrative label lists 6 g of protein per portion. How much is in two equal portions?
items.text: Two equal portions provide twice the listed amount.

items.title: Can a familiar bean dish be part of a protein-food routine?
items.text: Beans are a plant protein food.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Two similar foods have different labelled serving amounts. What should you do first? A. Pick the larger number. · B. Compare equal amounts. · C. Ignore both labels.
items.text: Equal amounts make the comparison useful.

items.title: An illustrative label shows 10 g of protein per 200 mL. You eat 100 mL. How much protein is that? A. 5 g. · B. 10 g. · C. 20 g.
items.text: Half the amount in this made-up example contains half the protein: 5 g.

items.title: You want an easier lunch. Which plan fits this lesson? A. Buy a supplement before checking your meals. · B. Remove every grain food. · C. Try a suitable protein food with other foods and plan safe storage.
items.text: Consider the full meal and whether you can carry and store it safely.

items.title: Write one sentence describing a food decision you can try, including how it will fit your day.
items.text: I will compare two similar bean products and pack my chosen one with a meal in a container that fits my bag.
